card.title: When two changes collide
card.blurb: Git joins two lines on its own until both sides changed the same file. Watch the merge stop with nothing saved, and see what it is waiting for.
hero.eyebrow: Git · Part three · Bringing work back
hero.title: When two changes collide
intro.0: The first time git says `CONFLICT` it looks like an accident - as if the merge failed and your work is in pieces somewhere. People who read it that way start undoing things at random, and that is how work actually gets lost. Nothing failed. Git merged every file it could on its own. Then it reached one it cannot decide for you, and stopped. Here you watch that moment, so a stopped merge never looks like a broken one again.
concept.gt-conflict.def: When both branches changed the same file, git stops and asks you to decide which result is right.
step.0.narr: One commit, `add dog`, and one name on it. Everything that follows grows out of this single point. Nothing here can collide yet - there is only one version of anything.
step.1.narr: Two lines now. On `fix` somebody saved `cat sleeps in the sun`, and back on `main` you saved `cat is hungry`. Read what each commit touched: **both of them changed `cat.txt`**.
step.2.narr: That last part is the whole difference. Two commits touching different files can both be kept - git just takes one of each. Two commits touching the same file leave a question git has no way to answer: which version of `cat.txt` should the joined line have?
step.2.note: Two versions of one file, and no rule to pick between them.
step.3.narr: Run `git merge fix` and watch the graph: **nothing was added**. No commit, no name moved. Git looked at both sides and found `cat.txt` changed on each one, so it stopped and left the decision to you. A conflict is git asking a question.
step.3.note: Git stopped. No commit was saved.
step.4.narr: The merge is only paused, and it is waiting on you. You say what `cat.txt` should end up as, tell git that file is settled, and commit. Now the merge commit appears, pointing back at both lines - the same shape a merge always ends in.
step.4.note: You decided; git saved the result.
step.5.narr: Nothing was ever damaged. Git finished every part it could work out alone and waited at the one it could not. Until you answer that question, no commit is made - which is why a conflict is safe to walk away from and come back to.
step.5.note: A conflict is a question, not a failure.
